raw:
Bea is not downstairs when you come out for lunch.

Nell and Owen occupy opposite ends of one of the café tables, each with their own food. Jo stands behind the counter with a supplier sheet, a calculator, and a pencil held between her teeth. You take the open place near the window and eat alongside them.

“I can do cheese toasties,” Jo says, removing the pencil, “but not at the price people expect them to be. Cheddar’s gone up again.”

Nell looks over the figures without taking the sheet. “What would make it workable?”

“A price I can live with after the card fees, the bread, and somebody asking for extra chutney.” Jo makes a note. “I’ll settle it tonight. I’m not printing a menu just because we’d all like one to exist.”

“That’s sensible,” Nell says.

Owen folds his sandwich wrapper into a neat square. “The pie was good, anyway.”

“It was supper,” Jo says. “Different standards. You’re not paying for my electricity at supper.”

Nell’s phone lights on the table. She checks the screen, then gathers her notebook. “I’ll be upstairs in five. Rowan, we can start on the programmes when you’re ready.”

Jo returns to her calculations. Owen takes his lunch things toward the kitchen, leaving the table quiet except for the faint traffic on Harbour Street beyond the glass.
